title: Whales evolved from four-legged land mammals related to hippos
body: Around 50 million years ago, the ancestors of whales were four-legged, even-toed mammals living near the shores of an ancient sea in what is now Pakistan and India. Fossils show a gradual move into the water over millions of years: legs shrank, nostrils shifted up the head to become blowholes, and tails turned into powerful flukes. Molecular studies show that their closest living relatives are hippopotamuses.

slides.heading: Oldest first
slides.explanation: Pakicetus, about 48.5 million years ago; Ambulocetus, about 48; Basilosaurus, about 41–34. Legs shrank and tails became flukes as the lineage took to the sea.

slides.heading: Pakicetus, ~48.5 Mya
slides.text: A wolf-like animal about 1–2 m long that lived in and around water. Its ear bones already had a shape found only in whales.

slides.heading: Ambulocetus, ~48 Mya
slides.text: The ‘walking whale’ had large feet and eyes on top of its head, and probably ambushed prey from the water’s edge much like a crocodile.

slides.heading: Basilosaurus, ~41–34 Mya
slides.text: A fully aquatic giant around 16 m long that still carried hind legs only about 35 cm long, far too small to walk on.

slides.heading: Basilosaurus: a giant with tiny legs
slides.note: About 41 to 34 million years ago; the legs were far too small to walk on
